lessons.title: What is a Godot game made of when it runs?
lessons.need: Open Godot for the first time and you see a Scene panel, a big view in the middle, and a list of several hundred node types. Before any script of yours runs, Godot has already decided what a game is made of and how its parts fit together. Every script in the later lessons is attached to one of those parts and runs because the part is in the game. So the question comes first: when you press Play, what is actually there? The manual answers it with four words, and this lesson takes them one at a time.
agenda: Scenes and nodes: what a game is built from.
The scene tree: where every part comes together when the game runs.
Signals: how one node tells others that something happened.

chunks.heading: Scenes
chunks.text:
The manual starts with one sentence that holds the whole lesson: “In Godot, a game is a tree of nodes that you group together into scenes. You can then wire these nodes so they can communicate using signals.”

“In Godot, you break down your game into reusable scenes. A scene can be a character, a weapon, a menu in the user interface, a single house, an entire level, or anything you can think of. Godot's scenes are flexible; they fill the role of both prefabs and scenes in some other game engines.”

“You can also nest scenes. For example, you can put your character in a level, and drag and drop a scene as a child of it.”

image.alt: The Scene dock: Game at the top, Level under it, Player under Level and Hook under Player. Level, Player and Hook each carry the clapperboard icon of a nested scene. Beside the dock, the character holds a hook in the 2D view.
image.caption: A character scene nested in a level, nested in the game.

check.prompt: Which of these can a Godot scene be?
choices: Only a character the player controls
A character, a weapon, a menu or a whole level
Only something drawn on the screen
check.why: The manual: a scene can be “a character, a weapon, a menu in the user interface, a single house, an entire level, or anything you can think of.”

chunks.heading: Nodes
chunks.text:
“A scene is composed of one or more nodes. Nodes are your game's smallest building blocks that you arrange into trees. Here's an example of a character's nodes.”

“It is made of a `CharacterBody2D` node named ‘Player’, a `Camera2D`, a `Sprite2D`, and a `CollisionShape2D`.” Build it below, one node at a time.

“The node names end with ‘2D’ because this is a 2D scene. Their 3D counterparts have names that end with ‘3D’.” The 3D base node is `Node3D`.

“Notice how nodes and scenes look the same in the editor. When you save a tree of nodes as a scene, it then shows as a single node, with its internal structure hidden in the editor.”

In the class reference, `Node` is the “Base class for all scene objects”, and a saved scene is a `PackedScene`: “An abstraction of a serialized scene.”

drawing.caption: The Player scene in the Scene dock

image.alt: The Scene dock with Player at the top and Camera2D, Sprite2D and CollisionShape2D under it; beside it, the 2D view shows a green square sprite.
image.caption: The same scene in the editor, from the manual.

check.prompt: You save the Player tree as a scene and add it to a level. How does it show in the level's Scene dock?
choices: As a single node, its insides hidden
As four separate nodes at the top of the level
As a file name with no icon
It does not show until the game runs
check.why: “When you save a tree of nodes as a scene, it then shows as a single node, with its internal structure hidden in the editor.”

chunks.heading: The scene tree
chunks.text:
“All your game's scenes come together in the scene tree, literally a tree of scenes. And as scenes are trees of nodes, the scene tree also is a tree of nodes. But it's easier to think of your game in terms of scenes as they can represent characters, weapons, doors, or your user interface.”

In the class reference, the `SceneTree` “Manages the game loop via a hierarchy of nodes.” That is the answer to this lesson's question: when the game runs, Godot runs one tree, and every scene you made is a branch of it.

image.alt: The Scene dock of a level: Level01 at the root with BackgroundLayer, InterfaceLayer, a TileMap, a CharacterBody2D, Portal2D, Coins and Enemies under it. UserInterface, CharacterBody2D and Portal2D carry the clapperboard icon of a nested scene.
image.caption: A level: other scenes nested as branches of one tree.

check.prompt: The scene tree is a tree of scenes. What else is it, in the manual's words?
check.why: “As scenes are trees of nodes, the scene tree also is a tree of nodes.”

chunks.heading: Signals
chunks.text:
“Nodes emit signals when some event occurs. This feature allows you to make nodes communicate without hard-wiring them in code. It gives you a lot of flexibility in how you structure your scenes.”

“For example, buttons emit a signal when pressed. You can connect a piece of code to this signal which will run in reaction to this event, like starting the game or opening a menu.”

“Other built-in signals can tell you when two objects collided, when a character or monster entered a given area, and much more. You can also define new signals tailored to your game.” In the class reference, a signal is a `Signal`.

image.alt: The Node dock's Signals tab for an Area2D: area_entered, area_exited, body_entered and more. body_entered has a connection under it to a function named _on_area_2d_body_entered.
image.caption: The signals one node can emit, one of them connected.

check.prompt: A button in your menu is pressed. What does the button do, in the manual's words?
choices: It calls every script in the tree
It saves the scene to disk
check.why: “Buttons emit a signal when pressed”, and code connected to that signal runs in reaction.

a.title: A character
a.text: The Player scene: a `CharacterBody2D` named Player with a `Camera2D`, a `Sprite2D` and a `CollisionShape2D` as its children. It moves, it is seen through its camera, it bumps into things.

image.alt: The Scene dock with Player at the top and Camera2D, Sprite2D and CollisionShape2D under it.
image.caption: The Player scene.

b.title: A menu
b.text: The manual's MainMenu scene: a menu in the user interface. Its tree holds a Background, a Context with texts, and a picture for each gamepad's start button. Nothing in it moves or collides.

image.alt: The Godot editor with a scene called MainMenu open: the Scene dock lists Background, MainScreen, Context, Texts, an HBoxContainer and pictures named XboxA, PlaystationX and NintendoB; the 2D view shows a title screen reading Harvester Game, Press enter to start.
image.caption: The MainMenu scene.

question.prompt: One is a character, the other a menu. What do the two share?
choices: Each is a tree of nodes saved as a scene
Each must have a camera to be seen
Each can only be used once in a game
Neither can be nested in another scene
question.why: A scene can be “a character, a weapon, a menu in the user interface”, and either way “a scene is composed of one or more nodes.”

exercises.prompt: You put your Player scene into the Level scene as a child, then press Play. What does the scene tree hold?
choices: The Level's nodes, with the Player's nodes as one branch
Only the Level's nodes; the Player stays in its own file
Two separate trees, one for each scene
exercises.why: “All your game's scenes come together in the scene tree”, so a nested scene is a branch of the one tree.

exercises.prompt: Type the missing class name. Godot's names are case-sensitive.
exercises.text: The manual's character “is made of a ____ node named ‘Player’, a `Camera2D`, a `Sprite2D`, and a `CollisionShape2D`.”
exercises.why: Player is a `CharacterBody2D`, the root of the character's tree.

exercises.prompt: Four notes on the Player scene. Which one is wrong?
lines: A scene is composed of one or more nodes.
Player, `Camera2D`, `Sprite2D` and `CollisionShape2D` form one tree.
Saved as a scene, Player shows as a single node in a level.
Nodes can only talk to each other through code wired between them.
exercises.fixed: Nodes emit signals, so they can communicate without hard-wiring them in code.
exercises.why: Signals exist so that nodes can “communicate without hard-wiring them in code.”

errors.what: An older tutorial tells you to add a “Spatial” node, and the Create New Node list has none.
errors.fix: Add a `Node3D`: “‘Spatial’ Nodes are now called ‘Node3D’ starting with Godot 4.”
errors.source: Godot manual, Overview of Godot's key concepts, the note under Nodes.

errors.what: “Confusion between a class and its instance.” In Godot: you treat the saved Player scene on disk and the Player in the running game as one and the same thing.
errors.fix: The saved scene is the plan; each time it is put in the tree, a new set of nodes is made from it, and those nodes are what runs.
errors.source: Sorva 2012, Table A.1, row 79 (Holland et al. 1997).

errors.what: “Objects are created by themselves, without explicit instructions to create them.” In Godot: you save a scene, press Play, and it is not in the game.
errors.fix: A node exists in the game only once it is in the tree, so nest the scene in your main scene (or instance it) before you run.
errors.source: Sorva 2012, Table A.1, row 91 (Détienne 1997; Ragonis & Ben-Ari 2005a).

lessons.exitStem: When a Godot game runs, it is made of …

lessons.title: What is a scene made of, and how do you run one?
lessons.need:
Lesson 0 said that a game is a tree of scenes and each scene is a tree of nodes. Now you build one. The manual's first scene holds a single node that draws “Hello World”, but the steps are the ones every scene goes through: pick a root node, set its properties, save it, run it.

One choice comes before all of them. An empty scene offers three ready-made root nodes, and the one you take decides what kind of scene you are making.
agenda: Nodes: what every node has, and how nodes form a tree.
Scenes: one root node, saved to disk, used as often as you like.
Your first scene: a `Label`, its Text property, running it, and the main scene.

chunks.heading: Nodes
chunks.text:
“Nodes are the fundamental building blocks of your game. They are like the ingredients in a recipe. There are dozens of kinds that can display an image, play a sound, represent a camera, and much more.”

“All nodes have the following characteristics: a name; editable properties; they receive callbacks to update every frame; you can extend them with new properties and functions; you can add them to another node as a child.”

“The last characteristic is important. Together, nodes form a tree, which is a powerful feature to organize projects. Since different nodes have different functions, combining them produces more complex behavior.”

image.alt: The Scene dock of a Main scene. Under Main: a Player with AnimatedSprite2D, CollisionShape2D, AudioStreamPlayer2D and Camera2D under it; an Enemy with AnimatedSprite2D, CollisionShape2D and an Area2D that holds its own CollisionShape2D; a CanvasLayer with a UI node.
image.caption: Many kinds of node, combined into one tree.

check.prompt: Which of these does every node have, in the manual's list?
check.why: The list starts “a name; editable properties”; a script, a picture or a camera depends on the kind of node.

chunks.heading: Scenes
chunks.text:
“When you organize nodes in a tree, like our character, we call this construct a scene. Once saved, scenes work like new node types in the editor, where you can add them as a child of an existing node. In that case, the instance of the scene appears as a single node with its internals hidden.”

“You can compose nodes to create custom and complex node types, like a game character that runs and jumps, a life bar, a chest with which you can interact, and more.”

“The Godot editor essentially is a scene editor. … A Godot project can contain as many of these scenes as you need. The engine only requires one as your application's main scene. This is the scene Godot will first load when you or a player runs the game.”

“On top of acting like nodes, scenes have the following characteristics: 1. They always have one root node, like the ‘Player’ in our example. 2. You can save them to your local drive and load them later. 3. You can create as many instances of a scene as you'd like.”

image.alt: The Scene dock of a 3D Player scene: Mannequiny (a nested scene), a CollisionShape3D, a StateMachine with Move, Idle, Air and Run under it, and a CameraRig scene. Beside it, the blue mannequin character in the 3D view.
image.caption: A character that runs and jumps, composed of nodes and nested scenes.

check.prompt: How many root nodes does a scene have?
choices: One for each kind of node in it
check.why: “They always have one root node, like the ‘Player’ in our example.”

chunks.heading: Three ways to start a scene
chunks.text:
“In an empty scene, the Scene dock on the left shows several options to add a root node quickly. 2D Scene adds a `Node2D` node, 3D Scene adds a `Node3D` node, and User Interface adds a `Control` node. These presets are here for convenience; they are not mandatory. Other Node lets you select any node to be the root node.”

“We're going to add a single `Label` node to our scene. Its function is to draw text on the screen.”

“A lot happens when you add a scene's first node. The scene changes to the 2D workspace because Label is a 2D node type. The Label appears, selected, in the top-left corner of the viewport. The node appears in the Scene dock on the left, and the node's properties appear in the Inspector dock on the right.”

image.alt: The Scene dock of an empty scene, under ‘Create Root Node:’: 2D Scene with a blue circle, 3D Scene with a red circle, User Interface with a green circle, and Other Node with a plus. The Add Child Node plus at the top left and Other Node are highlighted.
image.caption: An empty scene's root node choices.

check.prompt: In an empty scene you click User Interface. Which node becomes the root?
check.why: “User Interface adds a `Control` node”; 2D Scene adds a `Node2D` and 3D Scene a `Node3D`.

chunks.heading: Changing a property and running the scene
chunks.text:
“The next step is to change the Label's Text property. Let's change it to ‘Hello World’.” “You will see the text draw in the viewport as you type.”

“Everything's ready to run the scene! Press the Run Current Scene button in the top-right of the screen or press F6 (Cmd + R on macOS).”

“A popup invites you to save the scene, which is required to run it. Click the Save button in the file browser to save it as `label.tscn`.”

“The application should open in a new window and display the text ‘Hello World’.”

image.alt: The Inspector with the Label selected: under the Text property, the field reads Hello World.
image.caption: The Label's Text property, set in the Inspector.

check.prompt: You press Run Current Scene on a scene you have never saved. What happens first?
choices: A popup asks you to save it
Godot refuses and shows an error
It runs the main scene instead
check.why: “A popup invites you to save the scene, which is required to run it.”

chunks.heading: The main scene
chunks.text:
“To run our test scene, we used the Run Current Scene button. Another button next to it, Run Project, allows you to set and run the project's main scene. You can also press F5 (Cmd + B on macOS) to do so.”

“A popup window appears and invites you to select the main scene.” Pick `label.tscn`. “Moving forward, every time you run the project, Godot will use this scene as a starting point.”

“The editor saves the main scene's path in a project.godot file in your project's directory.”

image.alt: The run buttons at the top right of the editor. The first, a play triangle, is highlighted: Run Project. Pause, Stop and the buttons that run the current scene or a chosen scene follow it.
image.caption: Run Project, the first of the run buttons.

check.prompt: `label.tscn` is the main scene. You open another scene and press F5. What runs?
choices: Both scenes, one after the other
Nothing until you save the open scene
check.why: F5 is Run Project, and it runs the main scene; F6 runs the scene you have open.

a.title: The Hello World scene
a.text: One `Label` as the root and nothing under it. Its Text property says Hello World, and it is saved as `label.tscn`.

image.alt: The running game's window: a grey background with Hello World in white at the centre.
image.caption: The Hello World scene, running.

b.title: The character scene
b.text: A `CharacterBody2D` named Player as the root, with a `Sprite2D`, a `Camera2D` and a `CollisionShape2D` under it: “a playable character that the camera follows”.

drawing.caption: The character scene in the Scene dock

question.prompt: One scene has one node, the other four. What is true of both?
choices: Each has exactly one root node
Each needs a camera to run
Each must be the main scene
question.why: Scenes “always have one root node”: the `Label` in one, Player in the other.

exercises.prompt: You add a `Label` as the first node of an empty scene. Which workspace does the editor switch to?
exercises.why: “The scene changes to the 2D workspace because Label is a 2D node type.”

exercises.prompt: Type the missing class name. Godot's names are case-sensitive.
exercises.text: “We're going to add a single ____ node to our scene. Its function is to draw text on the screen.”
exercises.why: A `Label` draws text; its Text property holds the words.

exercises.prompt: Four notes on an empty scene's root choices. Which one is wrong?
lines: 2D Scene adds a `Node2D` as the root.
3D Scene adds a `Node3D` as the root.
User Interface adds a `Node2D` as the root.
Other Node lets you pick any node as the root.
exercises.fixed: User Interface adds a `Control` as the root.
exercises.why: The three presets give three different roots: `Node2D`, `Node3D` and `Control`.

exercises.prompt: You add the saved Hello World scene as a child in another scene. How does it show in that scene's dock?
choices: As a single node, its internals hidden
As the `Label` and every node under it
As a file name with no icon
It cannot be added to another scene
exercises.why: “The instance of the scene appears as a single node with its internals hidden”, as lesson 0 showed with the Player.

exercises.prompt: Your game has a level scene with the character scene nested in it, and the level is the main scene. The player starts the game. What does the scene tree hold?
choices: The level's nodes, with the character's nodes as one branch
Two trees, one for each scene
exercises.why: The main scene “is the scene Godot will first load”, and every scene nested in it comes together in the one scene tree (lesson 0).

errors.what: You press F5 and a different scene runs from the one you are editing.
errors.fix: F5 is Run Project and runs the main scene; press F6, Run Current Scene, to run the scene you have open.
errors.source: Godot manual, Nodes and Scenes, the note under Setting the main scene: “Running the project's main scene is distinct from running the current scene. If you encounter unexpected behavior, check to ensure you are running the correct scene.”

errors.what: The Save Scene As dialog will not let you save the scene outside your project's folder.
errors.fix: Save it inside the project: the `res://` path at the top of the window “represents the project's root directory and stands for ‘resource path’.”
errors.source: Godot manual, Nodes and Scenes, the note under Running the scene: the dialog “only allows you to save files inside the project.”

errors.what: “Difficulties with telling apart the static and dynamic aspects of programs.” In Godot: you read the Scene dock as the running game, and expect the `Label` to be on screen before you run anything.
errors.fix: The dock shows the scene as saved, the plan; the game is the window that opens when you press F6 or F5, built from that plan.

lessons.exitStem: A scene is made of …, and I run it by …

lessons.title: How can one scene appear many times in a game?
lessons.need:
A game rarely has one of anything: ten coins, six balls, a crowd of enemies. Building each one by hand would leave you six copies to keep in step every time you change your mind.

Godot's answer is that a saved scene is a blueprint, and every copy in the game is an instance made from it. This lesson follows the manual's ball: one scene, six instances that each fall on their own, and what happens when you change the blueprint or just one copy.
agenda: A saved scene as a blueprint, and instancing it.
Changing every instance through the scene, or one instance on its own.
Scenes as a way to plan a whole game.

chunks.heading: Packed scenes
chunks.text:
“In the previous part, we saw that a scene is a collection of nodes organized in a tree structure, with a single node as its root. You can split your project into any number of scenes.”

“You can create as many scenes as you'd like and save them as files with the `.tscn` extension, which stands for ‘text scene’. The `label.tscn` file from the previous lesson was an example. We call those files ‘Packed Scenes’ as they pack information about your scene's content.” In the class reference, such a file is a `PackedScene`.

“Here's an example of a ball. It's composed of a `RigidBody2D` node as its root named Ball, which allows the ball to fall and bounce on walls, a `Sprite2D` node, and a `CollisionShape2D`.”

image.alt: The Scene dock of the Ball scene: Ball at the top with a blue physics-body icon, Sprite2D and CollisionShape2D under it. Beside it, a light-blue ball in the 2D view.
image.caption: The Ball scene: a RigidBody2D root and two children.

check.prompt: Which node in the Ball scene lets the ball fall and bounce on walls?
check.why: The root is “a `RigidBody2D` node … which allows the ball to fall and bounce on walls”.

chunks.heading: Instancing
chunks.text:
“Once you have saved a scene, it works as a blueprint: you can reproduce it in other scenes as many times as you'd like. Replicating an object from a template like this is called instancing.”

“As we mentioned in the previous part, instanced scenes behave like a node: the editor hides their content by default. When you instance the Ball, you only see the Ball node. Notice also how each duplicate has a unique name.”

“Every instance of the Ball scene starts with the same structure and properties as `ball.tscn`. However, you can modify each independently, such as changing how they bounce, how heavy they are, or any property exposed by the source scene.”

image.alt: The Main scene's dock: WallContainer, then Ball, Ball2, Ball3, Ball4, Ball5 and Ball6, each with the clapperboard icon of an instanced scene. The 2D view shows six balls above purple walls.
image.caption: Six instances of one Ball scene, each with its own name.

check.prompt: You instance the Ball scene six times in Main. How many Ball scene files are there?
check.why: “Once you have saved a scene, it works as a blueprint”: the six balls are instances of one file.

chunks.heading: In practice
chunks.text:
“Let's add a ball as a child of the Main node. In the Scene dock, select the Main node. Then, click the link icon at the top of the scene dock. This button allows you to add an instance of a scene as a child of the currently selected node.”

“Now, we want to create more instances of the Ball node. With the ball still selected, press Ctrl + D (Cmd + D on macOS) to call the duplicate command.”

“Play the game again. You should now see every ball fall independently from one another. This is what instances do. Each is an independent reproduction of a template scene.”

image.alt: The top of the Scene dock with Main selected: the chain-link button next to the plus is highlighted.
image.caption: The link button adds an instance of a scene under the selected node.

check.prompt: Six balls fall in the running game, and one of them hits a wall first. What do the other five do?
choices: Keep falling, each on its own
Stop, since they share one body
check.why: “You should now see every ball fall independently from one another.”

chunks.heading: Editing scenes and instances
chunks.text:
“There is more to instances. With this feature, you can: 1. Change the properties of one ball without affecting the others using the Inspector. 2. Change the default properties of every Ball by opening the `ball.tscn` scene and making a change to the Ball node there. Upon saving, all instances of the Ball in the project will see their values update.”

“Changing a property on an instance always overrides values from the corresponding packed scene.”

“A grey ‘revert’ button appears next to the adjusted property.” “This icon indicates you are overriding a value from the source packed scene. Even if you modify the property in the original scene, the value override will be preserved in the instance. Clicking the revert icon will restore the property to the value in the saved scene.”

image.alt: The Gravity Scale row in the Inspector, set to 10.0, with the circular revert arrow beside its name highlighted.
image.caption: The revert button: this instance overrides the scene's value.

check.prompt: You set one ball's Gravity Scale to 10. Then you set Gravity Scale to 2 in `ball.tscn` and save. What is that one ball's Gravity Scale?
check.why: “Even if you modify the property in the original scene, the value override will be preserved in the instance.”

chunks.heading: Scene instances as a design language
chunks.text:
“We recommend dismissing architectural code patterns when making games with Godot, such as Model-View-Controller (MVC) or Entity-Relationship diagrams. Instead, you can start by imagining the elements players will see in your game and structure your code around them.”

“You can come up with a diagram like this for almost any type of game. Each rectangle represents an entity that's visible in the game from the player's perspective. The arrows point towards the instantiator of each scene.”

“Once you have a diagram, we recommend creating a scene for each element listed in it to develop your game. You'll use instancing, either by code or directly in the editor, to build your tree of scenes.”

image.alt: A diagram of a shooter game: boxes for Player Ship, Enemy, Obstacle, HUD, Weapon and Missile, with arrows pointing at Stage, the scene that instances them. A Weapon arrow points at Player Ship and a Market arrow at HUD; two dotted arrows are labelled ‘Instance by code’.
image.caption: A shooter broken down into scenes.

check.prompt: In the manual's scene diagram, what does each rectangle stand for?
choices: Something the player sees in the game
One class of an MVC pattern
check.why: “Each rectangle represents an entity that's visible in the game from the player's perspective.”

a.title: The Ball scene
a.text: One saved file, `ball.tscn`: a `RigidBody2D` named Ball with a `Sprite2D` and a `CollisionShape2D`. Change Bounce here and save, and every ball updates.

drawing.caption: The Ball scene in the Scene dock

b.title: Ball6, one instance in Main
b.text: Ball6 shows in Main as a single node. Its Gravity Scale was changed in the Inspector, so it keeps its own value whatever `ball.tscn` says.

image.alt: The editor with Main open: the Scene dock lists the walls and Ball to Ball6, with Ball6 selected. The Inspector shows Ball6 as a RigidBody2D with Gravity Scale 4.0; the 2D view shows the balls above the walls, Ball6 highlighted.
image.caption: Ball6 selected in Main, its properties in the Inspector.

question.prompt: How do the Ball scene and Ball6 differ?
choices: The scene is the blueprint; Ball6 is one copy made from it, with its own changes
They are the same node shown in two places
Ball6 is a second scene file
A change to Ball6 changes every ball
question.why: A saved scene “works as a blueprint”, and “each is an independent reproduction of a template scene”.

exercises.prompt: You open `ball.tscn`, set Bounce to 0.5 and save. No instance has its own Bounce value. What happens to the balls in Main?
choices: None change until you instance them again
exercises.why: “Upon saving, all instances of the Ball in the project will see their values update.”

exercises.prompt: Type the missing class name. Godot's names are case-sensitive.
exercises.text: “We call those files ‘Packed Scenes’ as they pack information about your scene's content.” In the class reference, such a file is a ____.
exercises.why: A saved scene is a `PackedScene`, “an abstraction of a serialized scene”.

exercises.prompt: Four notes on the manual's two scenes so far. Which one is wrong?
lines: The Ball's root is a `RigidBody2D`, which lets it fall and bounce on walls.
The playable character is built on a `CharacterBody2D`, with a `Camera2D` that follows it.
Both scenes have a `Sprite2D` and a `CollisionShape2D` under the root.
The Ball's root is a `CharacterBody2D` named Ball.
exercises.fixed: The Ball's root is a `RigidBody2D` named Ball.
exercises.why: The falling, bouncing ball is a `RigidBody2D`; the `CharacterBody2D` is the root of the playable character.

exercises.prompt: You open `ball.tscn` itself. Which node is its root?
exercises.why: Scenes “always have one root node” (lesson 1); here it is “a `RigidBody2D` node as its root named Ball”.

exercises.prompt: Main is the main scene and holds six Ball instances. You press F5. What runs?
choices: Main, with the six balls as branches of its tree
Only the scene you have open
exercises.why: F5 runs the main scene (lesson 1), and every instance in it comes together in the one scene tree (lesson 0).

errors.what: On one ball instance, the values of its PhysicsMaterial cannot be changed.
errors.fix: “PhysicsMaterial is a resource”: right-click the Physics Material property in the Inspector and click Make Unique, then edit it for that instance.
errors.source: Godot manual, Creating instances, the note under Editing scenes and instances.

errors.what: “Two objects with the same value for a name attribute are the same object.” In Godot: you take two nodes both named Ball, in two different scenes, to be one node.
errors.fix: A name only labels a node among its siblings; every instance is a separate node with its own properties, whatever it is called.

errors.what: “Confusion between a class and its instance.” In Godot: you change one ball in Main and expect `ball.tscn` and every other ball to change with it.
errors.fix: A change on an instance stays on that instance; to change every ball, open `ball.tscn`, change the Ball node there and save.
errors.source: Sorva 2012, Table A.1, row 79 (Holland et al. 1997).

lessons.exitStem: One scene appears many times in a game because …

lessons.title: How does a script make a node move?
lessons.need:
So far every change came from the Inspector: you set a property, and it stays set. A game needs properties that change while it runs, many times a second, and that is what a script is for: a file attached to a node that adds code to it.

The manual's first script makes the Godot icon turn in circles. In a handful of lines it shows what every later script leans on: which class the script extends, which functions the engine calls without being asked, and how a property is changed a little on every frame.
agenda: `extends`: a script is a class that builds on its node's class.
`_init()` and `print()`: code the engine runs for you.

chunks.heading: Attaching a script
chunks.text:
“To create and attach a new script to our node, right-click on Sprite2D in the Scene dock and select Attach Script.” “Change the Template field from ‘Node: Default’ to ‘Object: Empty’ to start with a clean file. Leave the other options set to their default values and click the Create button to create the script.”

“Every GDScript file is implicitly a class. The `extends` keyword defines the class this script inherits or extends. In this case, it's `Sprite2D`, meaning our script will get access to all the properties and functions of the Sprite2D node, including classes it extends, like `Node2D`, `CanvasItem`, and `Node`.”

“Inherited properties include the ones you can see in the Inspector dock, like our node's `texture`.”

image.alt: The Attach Node Script window: Language GDScript, Inherits Sprite2D, Template Object: Empty (highlighted), Built-in Script off, Path res://sprite_2d.gd, and Create and Cancel buttons.
image.caption: Attaching an empty script to the Sprite2D.

check.prompt: Your script starts with `extends Sprite2D`. What can it use?
choices: The properties and functions of `Sprite2D`, `Node2D`, `CanvasItem` and `Node`
Only the lines written in the script
Only what `Sprite2D` adds, not its parents
Nothing until a second script is attached
check.why: The script gets “all the properties and functions of the Sprite2D node, including classes it extends”.

chunks.heading: Hello, world!
chunks.text:
“Let's break it down. The `func` keyword defines a new function named `_init`. This is a special name for our class's constructor. The engine calls `_init()` on every object or node upon creating it in memory, if you define this function.”

“GDScript is an indent-based language. The tab at the start of the line that says `print()` is necessary for the code to work.”

“Save the scene as `sprite_2d.tscn` if you haven't already, then press F6 (Cmd + R on macOS) to run it. Look at the Output bottom panel that expands. It should display ‘Hello, world!’.”

image.alt: The Output panel: the Godot version line, then Hello, world!, then --- Debugging process stopped ---.
image.caption: The Output panel after running the scene.

check.prompt: No line in your script calls `_init()`. Does “Hello, world!” appear when the scene runs?
choices: Yes: the engine calls `_init()` when it creates the node
No: a function runs only when your code calls it
Only after you press F5 a second time
Only in the editor, not in the game
check.why: “The engine calls `_init()` on every object or node upon creating it in memory, if you define this function.”

chunks.heading: Every frame
chunks.text:
Delete `_init()` again and add two member variables after the `extends` line.

“Member variables sit near the top of the script, after any ‘extends’ lines, but before functions. Every node instance with this script attached to it will have its own copy of the `speed` and `angular_speed` properties.”

“To move our icon, we need to update its position and rotation every frame in the game loop. We can use the `_process()` virtual function of the `Node` class. If you define it in any class that extends the Node class, like Sprite2D, Godot will call the function every frame and pass it an argument named `delta`, the time elapsed since the last frame.”

“Games work by rendering many images per second, each called a frame, and they do so in a loop.” “The engine and game developers do their best to update the game world and render images at a constant time interval, but there are always small variations in frame render times. That's why the engine provides us with this delta time value, making our motion independent of our framerate.”

check.prompt: Who calls `_process(delta)`, and how often?
choices: The Inspector, when a property changes
check.why: “Godot will call the function every frame and pass it an argument named `delta`.”

chunks.heading: Turning around
chunks.text:
“The `func` keyword defines a new function. After it, we have to write the function's name and arguments it takes in parentheses. A colon ends the definition, and the indented blocks that follow are the function's content or instructions.”

“The line inside the function, `rotation += angular_speed * delta`, increments our sprite's rotation every frame. Here, `rotation` is a property inherited from the class `Node2D`, which `Sprite2D` extends. It controls the rotation of our node and works with radians.”

“By convention, Godot's virtual functions, that is to say, built-in functions you can override to communicate with the engine, start with an underscore.”

image.alt: Animation: the Godot icon turning in place on a grey background.
image.caption: The icon turning in place.

check.prompt: `angular_speed` is `PI`. Each frame adds `angular_speed * delta` to `rotation`. About how far does the icon turn in one second?
choices: One `delta`, a tiny fraction of a turn
check.why: The `delta`s of one second add up to one second, so the icon turns `angular_speed` radians per second, whatever the frame rate.

chunks.heading: Moving forward
chunks.text:
Two more lines go inside `_process()`, under the `rotation` line.

“As we already saw, the `var` keyword defines a new variable. If you put it at the top of the script, it defines a property of the class. Inside a function, it defines a local variable: it only exists within the function's scope.”

“To make the node move forward, we start from the Vector2 class's constant `Vector2.UP`, a vector pointing up, and rotate it by calling the Vector2 method `rotated()`. This expression, `Vector2.UP.rotated(rotation)`, is a vector pointing forward relative to our icon. Multiplied by our `speed` property, it gives us a velocity we can use to move the node forward.”

“We add `velocity * delta` to the node's `position` to move it. The position itself is of type `Vector2`, a built-in type in Godot representing a 2D vector.”
chunks.code:
var velocity = Vector2.UP.rotated(rotation) * speed

position += velocity * delta

image.alt: Animation: the Godot icon running in circles across a grey background.
image.caption: Turning and moving forward: the icon runs in circles.

check.prompt: Where does the `velocity` variable exist?
choices: In every function of the script
In the Inspector, as a property
In every node of the scene
check.why: Declared with `var` inside a function, it is “a local variable: it only exists within the function's scope.”

a.title: The constructor, _init()
a.text: The constructor: the engine calls it once, when it creates the node in memory. Here it prints one line to the Output panel.

b.title: The frame function, _process(delta)
b.text: A virtual function the engine calls on every frame, passing the time since the last one. Here it turns the sprite a little each time.

question.prompt: What do `_init()` and `_process(delta)` share, and how do they differ?
choices: The engine calls both; `_init()` once at creation, `_process()` every frame
Your own code must call both
Both run once, when the scene is saved
question.why: Both start with an underscore, the mark of the “built-in functions you can override to communicate with the engine”; only `_process()` repeats each frame.

exercises.prompt: You change `var angular_speed = PI` to `var angular_speed = PI * 2` and run the scene. What do you see?
choices: The icon turns twice as fast
It turns one full turn, then stops
Nothing changes until you restart Godot
It moves forward instead of turning
exercises.why: Each frame adds `angular_speed * delta`, so doubling `angular_speed` doubles the turn per second.

exercises.prompt: Type the property that turns the sprite. GDScript names are case-sensitive.
exercises.why: `rotation` is “a property inherited from the class `Node2D`”, in radians; GDScript properties are snake_case.

exercises.prompt: The script should turn the icon on every frame, but it never turns. Which line is the bug?
lines: extends Sprite2D
var angular_speed = PI
func _init(delta):
rotation += angular_speed * delta
exercises.why: `_init()` runs once, when the node is created; the engine calls `_process(delta)` every frame and passes it `delta`.

exercises.prompt: You instance the sprite scene three times in another scene and run it. How many copies of `speed` exist?
choices: Three: each instance has its own
Four: one per instance and one in the file
exercises.why: “Every node instance with this script attached to it will have its own copy of the `speed` and `angular_speed` properties” (instances: lesson 2).

exercises.prompt: The script is attached to the Sprite2D in `sprite_2d.tscn`. When does the engine start calling its `_process()`?
choices: When the scene runs and the node is in the scene tree
When you select the node in the Scene dock
When you open the Script workspace
exercises.why: The saved file is the plan (lesson 1); the engine calls `_process()` on the node in the running game's tree.

errors.what: The editor highlights a line in red with the error “Indented block expected”.
errors.fix: Indent the lines inside the function with a tab: “GDScript is an indent-based language.”
errors.source: Godot manual, Creating your first script, the note under Hello, world!: “If you omit it or don't indent a line correctly, the editor will highlight it in red and display the following error message: ‘Indented block expected’.”

errors.what: “Difficulties distinguishing between actual and formal parameters. Confusion over where parameter values come from.” In Godot: you look for the line that calls `_process(delta)` to see where `delta` comes from, or try to call it yourself.
errors.fix: Nobody calls `_process(delta)` by hand: the engine calls it every frame and passes the time since the last frame as `delta`.
errors.source: Sorva 2012, Table A.1, row 41 (Hristova et al. 2003).

errors.what: “Primitive assignment stores equations or unresolved expressions.” In Godot: you read `rotation += angular_speed * delta` as a rule that keeps `rotation` tied to `angular_speed` from then on.
errors.fix: The line is worked out each time it runs and adds one number to `rotation`; it only keeps the icon turning because the engine runs it again on every frame.
errors.source: Sorva 2012, Table A.1, row 15 (Bayman & Mayer 1983 et al.).

lessons.exitStem: A script makes a node move by …

lessons.title: How does a script know which key the player is pressing?
lessons.need:
The icon from the last lesson runs in circles by itself. A game hands that control to the player: turn while they hold left or right, move while they hold up.

Nothing in a node changes by itself when a key goes down. The script has to ask, and the manual's way to ask on every frame is a single object that the whole game can reach. Its answer is yes or no, and an `if` turns that answer into a choice.
agenda: Two tools for input: the input callbacks and the `Input` singleton.
`Input.is_action_pressed()` and `if`: turning only while a key is held.
Moving forward only while up is held.

chunks.heading: Two tools
chunks.text:
“You have two main tools to process the player's input in Godot:”

“1. The built-in input callbacks, mainly `_unhandled_input()`. Like `_process()`, it's a built-in virtual function that Godot calls every time the player presses a key. It's the tool you want to use to react to events that don't happen every frame, like pressing Space to jump.”

“2. The `Input` singleton. A singleton is a globally accessible object. Godot provides access to several in scripts. It's the right tool to check for input every frame.”

“We're going to use the `Input` singleton here as we need to know if the player wants to turn or move every frame.”

image.alt: Animation: the Godot icon turning and moving across a grey background, steered with the arrow keys.
image.caption: Where this lesson ends: turn with left and right, move with up.

check.prompt: The player presses Space once to jump. Which tool does the manual recommend for that?
check.why: Callbacks are “the tool you want to use to react to events that don't happen every frame, like pressing Space to jump.”

chunks.heading: Turning with the arrow keys
chunks.text:
In `_process()`, the `rotation` line gives way to this:

“Our `direction` local variable is a multiplier representing the direction in which the player wants to turn. A value of `0` means the player isn't pressing the left or the right arrow key. A value of `1` means the player wants to turn right, and `-1` means they want to turn left.”

“A conditional statement starts with the `if` keyword in GDScript and ends with a colon. The condition is specifically the expression between the keyword and the colon at the end of the line.”

check.prompt: The player holds neither arrow key. What is `direction` when the `rotation` line runs?
choices: `0`, so the icon does not turn
Whatever it was on the last frame
check.why: Each frame starts with `var direction = 0`, and neither `if` changes it.

chunks.heading: Asking Input
chunks.text:
“To check if a key was pressed this frame, we call `Input.is_action_pressed()`. The method takes a text string representing an input action and returns `true` if the action is pressed …”

“The two actions we use above, ‘ui_left’ and ‘ui_right’, are predefined in every Godot project. They respectively trigger when the player presses the left and right arrows on the keyboard or left and right on a gamepad's D-pad.”

“You can see and edit input actions in your project by going to Project > Project Settings and clicking on the Input Map tab.”

“Finally, we use the `direction` as a multiplier when we update the node's `rotation`: `rotation += angular_speed * direction * delta`.”

check.prompt: The player holds the right arrow. What does `Input.is_action_pressed("ui_right")` return on that frame?
choices: Nothing: it waits for the key
check.why: It “returns `true` if the action is pressed”; ‘ui_right’ is “predefined in every Godot project”.

chunks.heading: Moving when pressing up
chunks.text:
“To only move when pressing a key, we need to modify the code that calculates the velocity.” The `var velocity` line becomes:

“We initialize the `velocity` with a value of `Vector2.ZERO`, another constant of the built-in Vector type representing a 2D vector of length 0.”

“If the player presses the ‘ui_up’ action, we then update the velocity's value, causing the sprite to move forward.” The `position += velocity * delta` line stays as it was.

“If you run the scene, you should now be able to rotate with the left and right arrow keys and move forward by pressing Up.”

check.prompt: The player lets go of Up. What is `velocity` on the next frame?
choices: The last velocity, so it glides on
check.why: Each frame starts with `var velocity = Vector2.ZERO`; only a held ‘ui_up’ changes it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text:
“In summary, every script in Godot represents a class and extends one of the engine's built-in classes. The node types your classes inherit from give you access to properties, such as `rotation` and `position` in our sprite's case.”

“In GDScript, the variables you put at the top of the file are your class's properties, also called member variables. Besides variables, you can define functions, which, for the most part, will be your classes' methods.”

“Godot provides several virtual functions you can define to connect your class with the engine. These include `_process()`, to apply changes to the node every frame, and `_unhandled_input()`, to receive input events like key and button presses from the users.”

“The `Input` singleton allows you to react to the player's input anywhere in your code. In particular, you'll get to use it in the `_process()` loop.”

check.prompt: `speed` sits at the top of the script; `velocity` is declared inside `_process()`. Which one is a member variable?
check.why: “The variables you put at the top of the file are your class's properties, also called member variables”; `velocity` is local to `_process()`.

a.title: The Input singleton
a.text: Asked on every frame inside `_process()`: is this action held right now? Right for turning and moving, which last as long as a key is down.

b.title: An input callback
b.text: `_unhandled_input()`: a virtual function “Godot calls every time the player presses a key.” Right for events that happen once, like a jump on Space.

question.prompt: Holding Up keeps the icon moving forward. Which tool fits that, and why?
choices: `Input.is_action_pressed()` in `_process()`: it is asked every frame
`_init()`: it runs when the key goes down
Either one: they are called at the same moments
question.why: The `Input` singleton is “the right tool to check for input every frame”; the callback reacts once to each press.

exercises.prompt: The player holds Left and Right together. What is `direction` when the `rotation` line runs?
exercises.why: Both conditions are `true`, so `direction` is set to `-1` and then to `1`; the later line wins.

exercises.prompt: Type the method that asks whether an action is held. GDScript names are case-sensitive.
exercises.why: `Input.is_action_pressed()` “takes a text string representing an input action and returns `true` if the action is pressed”.

exercises.prompt: Four notes on the two input tools. Which one is wrong?
lines: `_unhandled_input()` is a virtual function Godot calls when the player presses a key.
The `Input` singleton can be asked from anywhere in your code.
Jumping once on Space suits an input callback.
Checking on every frame whether Left is held suits `_unhandled_input()`.
exercises.fixed: Checking on every frame whether Left is held suits the `Input` singleton.
exercises.why: The `Input` singleton is “the right tool to check for input every frame”.

exercises.prompt: You delete `* delta` from the turning line, so it reads `rotation += angular_speed * direction`. What changes?
choices: The turn per second now depends on the frame rate, and is far faster
exercises.why: `delta` is what makes “our motion independent of our framerate” (lesson 3); without it the icon turns `angular_speed` radians every frame.

exercises.prompt: Two instances of the sprite scene sit in one scene, and the player holds Left. What happens?
choices: Both turn: each runs its own `_process()` and asks `Input`
They take turns, one frame each
exercises.why: Each instance is its own node running the same script (lesson 2), and the `Input` singleton is “a globally accessible object”.

errors.what: The icon still runs in circles on its own after you add the turning code.
errors.fix: Comment out the old `var velocity = Vector2.UP.rotated(rotation) * speed` and `position += velocity * delta` lines: “This will ignore the code that moved the icon's position in a circle without user input.”
errors.source: Godot manual, Listening to player input, the step after the turning code.

errors.what: “Values are updated automatically according to a logical context.” In Godot: you expect `velocity` to change by itself when Up is pressed, and write no `if`.
errors.fix: Nothing changes by itself: on every frame, ask `Input.is_action_pressed("ui_up")` in `_process()` and set `velocity` when it returns `true`.

errors.what: “Variables always receive a particular default value upon creation.” In Godot: you write `var velocity` with no value and expect it to start as a zero vector.
errors.fix: Give the variable its starting value yourself, as the manual does: `var velocity = Vector2.ZERO`.
errors.source: Sorva 2012, Table A.1, row 10 (du Boulay 1986; Samuray 1989).

lessons.exitStem: A script knows which key is pressed because …

lessons.title: How does one node make code run in another?
lessons.need:
A button is pressed, a timer runs out, the player's health reaches zero. Each is an event in one node that other nodes care about: the sprite should stop, the screen should show game over.

You could make every node look at every other one each frame, but then each would have to know where the others are and what they are called. The manual's answer is the signal: a message a node emits when something happens to it. The node that emits does not know who is listening, and the listener's function runs without any line of yours calling it.
agenda: Connecting a `Button`'s `pressed` signal in the editor.
Connecting a `Timer`'s `timeout` signal in code with `connect()`.

chunks.heading: Signals
chunks.text:
“In this lesson, we will look at signals. They are messages that nodes emit when something specific happens to them, like a button being pressed. Other nodes can connect to that signal and call a function when the event occurs.”

“Signals are a delegation mechanism built into Godot that allows one game object to react to a change in another without them referencing one another. Using signals limits coupling and keeps your code flexible.”

“For example, you might have a life bar on the screen that represents the player's health. When the player takes damage or uses a healing potion, you want the bar to reflect the change. To do so, in Godot, you would use signals.”

“To add a button to our game, we will create a new scene which will include both a `Button` and the `sprite_2d.tscn` scene we created in the Creating your first script lesson.” The root is a `Node2D`, from the 2D Scene button. Build it below.

drawing.caption: The new scene in the Scene dock

check.prompt: With a signal, one node reacts to a change in another. What must the two nodes know about each other?
choices: Nothing: they do not reference one another
check.why: Signals let “one game object … react to a change in another without them referencing one another.”

chunks.heading: Connecting a signal in the editor
chunks.text:
“Here, we want to connect the Button's ‘pressed’ signal to our Sprite2D, and we want to call a new function that will toggle its motion on and off.”

“You can connect signals in the Signals dock. Select the Button node and, on the right side of the editor, click on the tab named Signals next to the Inspector.” “Double-click the ‘pressed’ signal to open the node connection window.”

“There, you can connect the signal to the Sprite2D node. The node needs a receiver method, a function that Godot will call when the Button emits the signal. The editor generates one for you. By convention, we name these callback methods ‘_on_node_name_signal_name’. Here, it'll be ‘_on_button_pressed’.”

image.alt: The Connect a Signal to a Method window: From Signal, pressed(); under Connect to Script, Node2D with Sprite2D selected and Button; Receiver Method, _on_button_pressed; Advanced off; Connect and Cancel buttons.
image.caption: Connecting the Button's pressed signal to a method on the Sprite2D.

check.prompt: The `Button` emits `pressed`. Which function does Godot call?
choices: `_on_button_pressed()` on the Sprite2D, the receiver method
check.why: The receiver method is “a function that Godot will call when the Button emits the signal.”

chunks.heading: Toggling the motion
chunks.text:
The generated method holds only `pass`. The manual replaces it:

“Our Sprite2D moves thanks to code in the `_process()` function. Godot provides a method to toggle processing on and off: `Node.set_process()`. Another method of the Node class, `is_processing()`, returns `true` if idle processing is active. We can use the `not` keyword to invert the value.”

“This function will toggle processing and, in turn, the icon's motion on and off upon pressing the button.” “Run the current scene by pressing F6 (Cmd + R on macOS), and click the button to see the sprite start and stop.”

image.alt: Line 23 of the script, func _on_button_pressed() -> void:, with a green connection icon in the left margin; line 24 reads pass # Replace with function body.
image.caption: The generated method, marked with the connection icon.

check.prompt: The icon is moving. The player presses the button twice. What is the icon doing after the second press?
choices: Standing still for good: a connection fires once
check.why: Each press emits `pressed` again and runs the method again: the first press turns processing off, the second turns it back on.

chunks.heading: Connecting a signal via code
chunks.text:
“You can connect signals via code instead of using the editor. This is necessary when you create nodes or instantiate scenes inside of a script.” “Godot has a `Timer` node that's useful to implement skill cooldown times, weapon reloading, and more.” Add one under the Sprite2D and turn on its Autostart property.

“We want to connect the signal when the scene is instantiated, and we can do that using the `Node._ready()` built-in function, which is called automatically by the engine when a node is fully instantiated.” “The function `get_node()` looks at the Sprite2D's children and gets nodes by their name.”

“The line reads like so: we connect the Timer's ‘timeout’ signal to the node to which the script is attached. When the Timer emits `timeout`, we want to call the function `_on_timer_timeout()`, that we need to define.”

“The `visible` property is a boolean that controls the visibility of our node. The line `visible = not visible` toggles the value. If `visible` is `true`, it becomes `false`, and vice-versa.” “If you run the Node2D scene now, you will see that the sprite blinks on and off, at one second intervals.”

image.alt: The Scene dock: Node2D at the root, Sprite2D under it with a Timer as its child, then Button, which shows a signal-connection icon.
image.caption: The Timer added as a child of the Sprite2D.

check.prompt: `_ready()` runs once and makes the connection. When does `_on_timer_timeout()` run?
choices: Never: no line of the script calls it
check.why: “When the Timer emits `timeout`, we want to call the function `_on_timer_timeout()`”: the connection says what to call, the signal says when.

chunks.heading: Custom signals
chunks.text:
“You can define custom signals in a script. Say, for example, that you want to show a game over screen when the player's health reaches zero. To do so, you could define a signal named ‘died’ or ‘health_depleted’ when their health reaches 0.” “As signals represent events that just occurred, we generally use an action verb in the past tense in their names.”

“Your signals work the same way as built-in ones: they appear in the Signals tab and you can connect to them like any other.” “To emit a signal in your scripts, call `emit()` on the signal.”

“Any node in Godot emits signals when something specific happens to them, like a button being pressed. Other nodes can connect to individual signals and react to selected events.” “For example, an `Area2D` representing a coin emits a `body_entered` signal whenever the player's physics body enters its collision shape, allowing you to know when the player collected it.”
chunks.code:
extends Node2D

signal health_depleted

var health = 10


func take_damage(amount):
	health -= amount
	if health <= 0:
		health_depleted.emit()

image.alt: The Signals tab: under custom_signal.gd, health_depleted(); under CanvasItem, draw() and hidden().
image.caption: A custom signal, listed above the built-in ones.

check.prompt: `health` is 10, and `take_damage(4)` is called three times. When is `health_depleted` emitted?
choices: On the third call, when `health` drops to -2
Never: only the engine emits signals
check.why: 10, 6, 2, then -2: only the third call makes `health <= 0` true and reaches `emit()`.

a.title: Connected in the editor
a.text: The `Button`'s `pressed` signal, joined to `_on_button_pressed()` on the Sprite2D in the Signals dock. The editor wrote the method and marks it with a connection icon.

b.title: Connected in code
b.text: The `Timer`'s `timeout` signal, joined in `_ready()` with `connect()`. Needed when nodes are made or scenes instanced from a script.

question.prompt: What do the two connections have in common?
choices: Each runs a method on one node whenever another node emits a signal
Each runs its method once, when the connection is made
question.why: Editor or code, a connection joins a signal to a receiver method, which runs each time the signal is emitted.

exercises.prompt: You rename the Timer node to BlinkingTimer in the Scene dock and change nothing in the script. What happens when the scene runs?
choices: `get_node()` finds no node named Timer, so nothing gets connected
Godot follows the rename by itself
exercises.why: `get_node()` “gets nodes by their name”: after a rename “you would have to change the call to `get_node("BlinkingTimer")`.”

exercises.prompt: Type the method that joins the signal to the function. GDScript names are case-sensitive.
exercises.why: “To connect to a signal via code, you need to call the `connect()` method of the signal you want to listen to.”

exercises.prompt: Four notes on the scene's nodes and signals. Which one is wrong?
lines: `Button` is a node; `pressed` is a signal it emits.
`Timer` is a node; `timeout` is a signal it emits.
`_on_button_pressed()` is the receiver method on the Sprite2D.
`pressed` is a node you add under the `Button`.
exercises.fixed: `pressed` is the signal the `Button` emits when it is pressed.
exercises.why: Nodes are what you add to the tree; signals are the messages nodes “emit when something specific happens to them”.

exercises.prompt: This script should tell its listeners when health runs out, but nothing ever reacts. Which line is the bug?
lines: signal health_depleted
func take_damage(amount):
health -= amount
health_depleted.connect()
exercises.why: “To emit a signal in your scripts, call `emit()` on the signal”; `connect()` joins a listener, it sends nothing.

exercises.prompt: The button's method calls `set_process(false)`. What happens to the sprite's `_process(delta)`?
choices: The engine stops calling it, so the icon stops
It runs once more, then stops
It is removed from the script
exercises.why: The engine calls `_process()` every frame (lesson 3) only while processing is on; `set_process()` turns it on and off.

exercises.prompt: Two instances of `sprite_2d.tscn` sit under the Node2D, and only the first one's `_on_button_pressed()` is connected to the `Button`. The player presses it. What stops?
exercises.why: Each instance is its own node (lesson 2), and a connection joins the signal to one receiver.

errors.what: You connect a signal in the Signals dock while writing scripts in an external editor such as VS Code, and no receiver method appears.
errors.fix: Connect the signal in code with `connect()`, as in the `Timer` example.
errors.source: Godot manual, Using signals, the note under Connecting a signal in the editor: “this automatic code generation might not work. In this case, you need to connect the signal via code.”

errors.what: “Difficulties understanding the invocation of a method from another method.” In Godot: you expect `_on_timer_timeout()` to run when `timer.timeout.connect(_on_timer_timeout)` runs in `_ready()`.
errors.fix: `connect()` only makes the link; the method runs each time the `Timer` emits `timeout`, once a second here.

errors.what: “A (Java) method must always be invoked on an explicit object.” In Godot: you search the script for the line that calls `_on_button_pressed()`, find none, and decide the method never runs.
errors.fix: No line of yours calls a receiver method: Godot calls it on the receiver node each time the `Button` emits `pressed`.

lessons.exitStem: One node makes code run in another by …

table.caption: Course 1's last check: three base nodes, three questions. Answer each cell in your head, then tap it to see the class reference's answer.

rows.head: Node2D
cells: It can: it is a `CanvasItem`, and “Any CanvasItem can draw.”
Yes, in 2D: “Has a position, rotation, scale, and skew.”
The one scene tree, with every other node; it is drawn on the 2D canvas.

rows.head: Control
cells: It can: it is a `CanvasItem` too, the base of the interface nodes.
Yes: it “Adapts its position and size based on its parent control.”
The same scene tree; it is drawn on the 2D canvas, like `Node2D`.

rows.head: Node3D
cells: Not by itself: it is the “Base object in 3D space”; nodes that draw in 3D inherit from VisualInstance3D, the “Parent of all visual 3D nodes.”
Yes, in 3D: its translation, rotation and scale are “relative to the parent”.
The same scene tree; it is placed in the 3D world.
